title: AI Usage & Prompt Engineering
heading: AI Usage & Prompt Engineering
summary: This course introduces students to the rapidly developing world of AI, with an emphasis on the large language models (LLMs) that power today's AI assistants — like OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google's Gemini, and Anthropic's Claude. These tools are now multimodal: alongside text, they can understand images, listen and speak, work with documents, and generate images of their own. Designed for beginners, the course covers the practical skills for engaging with AI responsibly and effectively.
objectives: Understand the basics of Generative AI, especially LLMs, and their role in generative tasks.
Practice ethical usage of Generative AI.
Learn clear communication strategies with Generative AI, called "prompt engineering."
Apply Generative AI tools in practical scenarios for creativity, learning, and productivity.

units.title: Unit 1: Fundamentals of AI
units.description: How generative AI works under the hood — from neural networks and training to the LLMs and image models behind today's AI assistants.

slides: Intro to Generative AI

What is AI?

AI has become such a buzzword in recent years that it can be hard to nail down its exact definition, which is actually pretty broad.

AI, or artificial intelligence, refers to the simulation of human intelligence processes by a computer algorithm. This definition encompasses all sorts of different systems.

All images generated by DALL·E 3

What is AI?

Some of these intelligence processes include learning (gaining information), reasoning (using rules to reach conclusions), and self-correction.

It does not have anything to do with sentience or self-awareness, but rather the ability of an algorithm to solve problems by adjusting its own parameters to improve performance. This is called machine learning.

What is generative AI?

Generative AI refers to AI models that generate new data similar to the data they were trained on.

Unlike older AI models that mostly focused on classification or prediction, generative models aim to create new content, whether it's text, images, or other forms of data.

How does generative AI work?

Generative AI models are trained on huge amounts of data, learning the underlying patterns and relationships.

During the training process, the model adjusts its parameters to minimize the “loss function” (the difference between the generated outputs and the desired outputs). Once trained, the model can generate new data instances when given an input prompt.

How does generative AI work?

Large Language Models (LLMs) like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini are some of the most popular generative AI models. These models are trained on gigantic sets of text from the internet and other sources. By learning the underlying patterns and structures of language, LLMs can generate human-like responses to text prompts.

How does generative AI work?

Text-to-image models like DALL·E and Midjourney work in a similar way, except they transform text input into images rather than text. They are trained on image-caption pairs and learn to associate words with millions of different visual properties.

How does generative AI work?

Generative AI models are usually neural networks, which are made of layers of interconnected nodes called “neurons”. They behave like a simplified version of the neurons in your brain, in that they respond to input stimuli and transmit output signals.

Neural networks use this cascading effect to transform an input signal into an appropriate output.

How a neural network is trained

Data Gathering

The first step in training a neural network is to collect a large and diverse dataset that represents the “problem domain” (for example, images with captions). The data is preprocessed to clean it and transform it into a format suitable for training.

Initialization

A suitable neural network architecture is chosen based on the nature of the problem. The model's initial parameters, such as weights and biases, are usually set randomly.

Forward Pass

Input data is fed through the network, and predictions are made. At first, the model essentially has to guess randomly and is usually very wrong. The model’s output is compared to the expected “correct” output using a loss function.

Backpropagation

The error signal is propagated backward through the network, and the model's parameters are adjusted to minimize the loss using optimization algorithms like gradient descent. Then we do another forward pass and repeat the process.

How a neural network is trained

During the forward pass / backpropagation loop, the model is validated or evaluated on a separate dataset (data that was not used during training) to monitor and fine-tune performance. This also helps developers decide when to stop training the model.

If a model is trained for too long there is a risk of overfitting, which is when the model learns the training data “too well”. A model that is overfitted to training data will start to perform more poorly against testing data, because it has learned to spot random patterns (noise) that only exist in the training data. This makes it harder for the model to generalize.

AI Misconception #1

“AI can only copy existing data.”

While generative AI can mimic training data, it can also create entirely novel ideas based on patterns it has learned from its training data. The AI model works within its own model of reality called a "latent space," which is a multi-dimensional compressed representation of everything it has learned during training.

AI Misconception #2

“AI always tells the truth.”

AI models are far from perfect and often generate outputs that are false or nonsensical. They don’t "lie" in the human sense; lying implies intent to deceive, which AI lacks. Instead, outputs can be inaccurate due to limitations in the model or the training data. It has no capability of distinguishing between truth and lies.

AI Misconception #3

“AI models are unbiased.”

AI systems will inherit and perpetuate any biases in the data used to train them. In other words, an AI model is as objective as the dataset used to train it; no more, no less. These biases can lead to unfair or discriminatory results.

AI Misconception #4

“AI will replace us all!”

While AI has the potential to automate certain tasks and jobs, it’s not going to completely replace us any time soon. Some jobs will be replaced, some will become easier for us, and some new jobs will be created. This is a cycle that repeats whenever a game-changing technology emerges.

See: the Industrial Revolution, the Internet, etc.

AI Misconception #5

“AI will lead to superintelligent machines taking over the world.”

AI research has made significant strides, but even human-level general intelligence is still a far distant goal. Concerns about AI posing existential threats are speculative and highly sensationalized. That said, there are still plenty of ongoing discussions about safety and ethics.

units.title: Unit 2: Ethical AI Usage
units.description: Overview of AI and ethics of engagement for generative purposes.

slides: AI Ethics

What is “ethics”?

Ethics is the philosophical study of morals. It asks the question, “how should we live?” In other words, what are the “shoulds” and “should nots” of society?

Ethics allows us to navigate the complexities of right and wrong, fair and unfair. It mirrors our collective conscience and acts like a compass for behavior in society.

All images generated by DALL·E 3

Ethics in the age of AI

The ongoing rise of generative AI has unleashed a number of new and complicated moral questions, both for developers and for users. And as the pace of AI improvement accelerates, these challenges will snowball. It’s important to answer these questions as we move forward.

Ethical AI Development

What responsibilities do AI developers have?

Core principles of AI ethics

#1. Transparency

AI systems should be clear and understandable by humans. Clarity allows for trust and accountability.

For example, an AI loan approval system that explains its decisions based on credit history and income, allowing applicants to understand and trust the process.

Core principles of AI ethics

#2. Fairness

AI should not perpetuate or amplify biases, intentionally or not.

A real-world negative example: an AI recruitment tool used by Amazon was found to be biased against women. The system favored male candidates over female candidates for technical roles.

Core principles of AI ethics

#3. Privacy

AI should respect and protect individuals' privacy.

For example, a smart assistant that listens to your voice (like Alexa or Siri) should not keep recordings of what you say or sell your data to advertisers without your explicit permission.

Core principles of AI ethics

#4. Accountability

Developers and deployers of AI are accountable for its actions.

If an AI system is found to pose danger to humans in any way, the company that deployed it is responsible for correcting it immediately.

Ethical AI Usage

What responsibilities do you and I have?

How to use AI responsibly

Learn how it works

Understand the purpose and the limitations of the AI systems you use. Be aware of what data you’re sharing and configure your privacy settings to protect personal information.

Use it as a tool

Use AI to study for a test, not to cheat on your homework. The line between these two can seem blurry sometimes, but it’s helpful to ask yourself: “is this helping me learn the subject, or is it just letting me pass the class?”

Avoid plagiarism

Even though AI produces unique content, it might copy copyrighted writing or intellectual property. Be careful about copy-pasting text from ChatGPT. Instead, use it as a study buddy, and then write in your own words.

Own your actions

Much like AI developers are responsible for making sure it doesn’t cause harm, users are responsible for the way they use AI. Using AI to indirectly harm others is the same as doing it yourself. This includes cyberbullying and spreading disinformation.

Slideshow - Prompt Engineering vs. Problem Formulation

slides: Prompt Engineering vs. Problem Formulation

What is prompt engineering?

Prompt engineering is a set of strategies used to get better results from your generative AI prompts.

While AI models have made great strides recently, they’re still far from perfect. Many users have tried to develop strategies that give them better results.

All images generated by DALL·E 3

Prompt engineering tips

#1. Be clear and precise

The more vague your prompt is, the more vague the AI’s response will be. Be as direct and specific as possible. Remember that you’re not talking to a mind reader, or a human for that matter. AI models can’t always read between the lines as well as you might expect.

Prompt engineering tips

#2. Iterate

To “iterate” means to repeat and improve a process over time.

Start with a basic prompt, see how it performs, look for errors, improve it, and repeat. Swap out words and sharpen your prompt until you get the results you want. Take note of how your changes impacted the result.

Prompt engineering tips

#3. Itemize

Break complex multi-step tasks into small manageable pieces. AI models do better with step-by-step instructions, much like people.

For example, instead of asking it to write you a children’s book, ask it to give you a rough outline, and then use that outline to have it write one page at a time.

Prompt engineering tips

#4. Provide examples

If you need the AI to answer you in a specific way, it can be helpful to give it an example of what a good answer looks like.

For example: “Make me an ‘80s New Wave music playlist. Here is an example of what your answer should look like: …” and show it how you’d like it to be formatted.

Prompt engineering tips

#5. Role prompting

Sometimes it helps to begin your conversation by giving the AI a role.

“You are a professional career coach.”

“You are an expert computer hardware technician.”

“You are a 5-star chef.”

Prompt engineering tips

#6. Avoid negation statements

Sometimes, AI models get confused when asked not to do something. If I asked you to not think about elephants, you’d probably think about elephants.

Rather than asking the AI model NOT to do something, ask it to DO the thing you need it to do.

Example

“draw a city without any cars”

“draw a city with only bikes and pedestrians”

Neither prompt produced perfect results, but the second prompt did much better. Telling DALL·E not to draw cars actually made it difficult for it to avoid drawing cars. If you’re having trouble getting the results you want, try rephrasing your negation statements into positive assertions.

Prompt engineering tips

#7. Use delimiters

A delimiter is a sequence of characters that helps to visually separate different parts of text.

For example, you might use symbols like ```triple backticks``` or <angle brackets> to help the AI distinguish between different parts of your prompt.

An example of using delimiters in a prompt

Limitations of prompt engineering

Here’s the thing: all of the tips and tricks we’ve discussed seem to work in certain scenarios, but they’re not bulletproof.

The field of generative AI is advancing and changing extremely rapidly. It’s very likely that AI models will very soon become so effective that most of these tips and tricks will have to be modified. Some might not work the same way at all.

More importantly, no amount of prompt engineering will help as long as the user isn’t able to communicate what they actually want.

What is problem formulation?

Problem formulation is a powerful communication skill. It’s the ability to accurately and precisely define a problem. It’s about understanding the problem you’re trying to solve.

Sometimes the problem isn’t in the way you’re phrasing your question; it’s in not fully understanding the question in the first place.

Steps to effective problem formulation

Identify the “problem”. Clearly define what you actually want generative AI to accomplish in this scenario, whether it’s answering a difficult question or helping you create something new.

Understand the context. Gather background information and learn about the constraints specific to your problem.

Steps to effective problem formulation

Break Down the Problem. Decompose it into smaller, manageable parts. Sometimes it’s better to solve it one piece at a time. Maybe start with an outline of the problem and go from there.

Develop Hypotheses. Try to come up with possible solutions on your own, and then use these to guide your prompts.

Integrate both approaches!

As you sharpen your problem-solving and communication skills, you will be more capable of using generative AI as a tool rather than a crutch.
